title: The insult
hookLine: it isn't the insulter who harms you but your judgment that you're harmed (Enchiridion 20)

cards: A man in the street kicks Socrates. His friends are outraged and want him to take the man to court. Socrates shrugs.
If a donkey had kicked me, he asks, would I sue the donkey? The story is told in Diogenes Laertius' Lives of the Philosophers. Not everyone manages that shrug.
Somebody cuts in front at the pharmacy and calls you something under their breath, and for the rest of the afternoon you're writing speeches to them in your head.
Section twenty of the handbook asks where, exactly, the injury happened.

teach.h: NOT THE INSULTER, BUT YOUR JUDGMENT.
teach.b: Remember, Epictetus says, that it isn't the one who abuses you or hits you who insults you. It's your judgment about them, that they've insulted you. The Greek verb is from hybris, outrage, the word behind our hubris.
The outrage, he says, is completed inside. So when someone provokes you, know that it's your own judgment that has provoked you. That sounds like blaming the victim, and it's worth slowing down here.
Epictetus isn't saying the person behaved well, or that you shouldn't defend yourself or others from real harm.
He's talking about the second injury, the one that keeps going all afternoon: the speeches in your head. That part, he says, runs on your verdict, and it can be looked at. Then the tool.
Try above all, he says, not to be carried off by the impression.
If you once gain time and delay, you'll more easily master yourself. Time and delay. A breath.
A count of three. Going to the window before answering the email.
Seneca, writing a whole essay on anger, said much the same: delay is the greatest remedy for anger. It's one of the places where the Stoic writers agree closely. The first flash is fast and hot.
Many people find that if they give it a few seconds, it often cools enough for them to choose. Not suppressing anything.
Just one breath between the sting and the reply.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism pause, even for a single breath, before replying to an insult, giving the first flash of anger time to cool.

o: a wrong completed by your own judgment of it
a formal charge brought against you in court
any harsh word, which always does real harm

p: delay is the remedy for anger

s: Epictetus says the person who insults you behaved well
he says the lasting injury runs on your judgment; he doesn't excuse them.
he says gaining time and delay helps you master yourself
don't be carried off by the first impression.
Seneca wrote a whole essay on anger
and said delay is its greatest remedy.

games.q: someone in line mutters an insult at you. what does Epictetus suggest first?
o: gain a little time before reacting.
pretend you didn't hear and stew all day.
games.why: if you once gain time and delay, he says, you'll more easily master yourself.

practice: Remember a moment when someone said something that stung, and let it replay once: the heat rising, the reply forming. At the exact point where you would answer, stop, and take one slow breath in and out.
Notice what's different on the other side of it; maybe the reply is the same, maybe it's softer, or unnecessary.

wordCard.voice: The insult. In Epictetus' handbook, completed not by the one who abuses you but by your judgment that you've been harmed, and loosened by a little delay. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 20 (as the verb hubrizei): outrage, insult; the root of hubris.

carryVoice: Your line: a breath before. The sting comes fast; the answer can come after. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
